articles.title: Scientists create a remarkable new rechargeable battery using vitamin B12
articles.summary: Scientists have found a surprising new use for vitamin B12, developing a rechargeable battery that uses the essential nutrient to help generate and store electricity. The prototype survived up to 250 charging cycles and could open the door to safer, cheaper, and more environmentally friendly alternatives to lithium-ion batteries.
articles.content:
Scientists have found an unexpected new use for vitamin B12, a nutrient best known for its importance to human health. Researchers at the University of Córdoba have incorporated the vitamin into a rechargeable battery, demonstrating for the first time that it can serve as a catalyst in this type of energy storage system.

Vitamin B12 is essential for normal bodily function and is naturally present in animal products. The vitamin is produced by certain bacteria, which occur in nature and are also grown commercially to supply the food and pharmaceutical industries. In addition to its established applications in medicine, nutrition, and veterinary care, B12 is used to address certain nutritional deficiencies. It has also become popular alongside other B vitamins as a hangover remedy because of its potential to help reduce fatigue.

Now, scientists are exploring an entirely different application. By using the vitamin to support the chemical reactions inside a battery, they have developed a prototype capable of completing up to 250 charging and discharging cycles.

How Vitamin B12 Makes a Rechargeable Battery Possible

The new battery was developed by the Physical Chemistry research group (FQM-204) at the University of Córdoba's Chemical Institute for Energy and the Environment (IQUEMA). It uses zinc and oxygen from the surrounding air to produce electricity, with vitamin B12, also called cobalamin, playing a crucial role in the process.

To make the design work, the researchers attached vitamin B12 molecules to single-walled carbon nanotubes. The vitamin contains cobalt (III) at its center, which helps drive the electrochemical reactions needed for the battery to function.

The team has previously experimented with natural molecules as battery catalysts, including hemoglobin and catalase. These substances contain iron (II) and iron (III), respectively. Vitamin B12 represents the group's third effort to use a biological molecule for this purpose, but it has delivered an important advance: a battery that can be recharged repeatedly, completing as many as 250 cycles.

One of the biggest obstacles was keeping vitamin B12 inside the battery. Because the vitamin dissolves readily in water, it would normally be difficult to retain in a system that relies on a water-based electrolyte.

The researchers overcame this problem by securing the vitamin to carbon nanotubes, using an approach inspired by how amino acids connect to form proteins.

Manuel Cano Luna, one of the study's authors, explained that "we looked at the properties we can find in naturally occurring materials to use them in new batteries," while describing the team's search for useful biological compounds.

Their attachment technique imitates "the process by which amino acids bind together in proteins."

Alongside Cano Luna, the research team included Valentín García Caballero, Miguel López León, Pablo Gómez Argudo, Luis Camacho Delgado, José Miguel Rodríguez Mellado, María Teresa Martín Romero, José Abad López, and Antonio Jesús Fernández Romero.

A Safer, Lighter Alternative to Lithium-Ion Batteries

The findings, published in the Journal of Materials Chemistry A, could contribute to the development of battery technologies that depend less on the materials used in conventional lithium-ion batteries.

Although lithium-ion batteries are widely used, obtaining their raw materials can involve significant economic, environmental, and social challenges. Zinc-air batteries offer a potential alternative because they can store substantial amounts of energy relative to their weight while relying on materials that are more readily available.

Zinc is abundant and recyclable, and these batteries use oxygen from the surrounding atmosphere as part of their energy-producing reactions. Because they draw oxygen from the air rather than storing all the necessary reactants internally, they can also be lighter than other battery designs.

This advantage has helped make zinc-air batteries increasingly useful in compact electronic devices, particularly hearing aids. Another benefit is their use of non-flammable, water-based electrolytes, which can reduce fire risks and improve safety.

Why Vitamin B12 Is Key to Recharging

A major challenge in developing rechargeable zinc-air batteries is finding a catalyst that can efficiently support the chemical reactions involved in both producing and storing electricity.

During discharge, the battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy. Recharging requires the relevant chemical reactions to proceed in the opposite direction. A suitable catalyst must therefore be effective in both processes.

According to researcher Antonio Jesús Fernández Romero, vitamin B12 "has proven to meet the necessary conditions to act as a good catalyst because, during discharge, it catalyzes the reduction of oxygen to water and, during recharging, it promotes the production of oxygen."

This ability to support both reactions is what makes the vitamin particularly promising for rechargeable zinc-air battery technology.

Could Vitamin B12 Help Store Renewable Energy?

The successful prototype offers a new direction for researchers seeking affordable, sustainable alternatives to existing energy storage technologies.

If the approach can be developed further, batteries using vitamin B12 catalysts could eventually help address one of the biggest challenges facing renewable energy: storing excess electricity generated by sources such as solar and wind power for use when production falls.

Although the technology remains at the research stage, demonstrating up to 250 charge and discharge cycles shows that a familiar biological molecule can play an unexpected role in rechargeable battery design. The discovery adds to growing efforts to use naturally occurring substances to create safer, lighter, and more sustainable ways to store energy.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough where vitamin B12 is used as a catalyst in rechargeable zinc-air batteries, offering a safer, cheaper, and more environmentally friendly alternative to lithium-ion batteries. This innovation has broad implications for sustainable energy storage, potentially aiding renewable energy adoption and reducing reliance on scarce or problematic materials. The story is focused, detailed, and highlights a tangible advancement with meaningful societal and environmental impact.

articles.title: Pakistan's solar revolution is so successful the national grid is lagging behind
articles.summary: People installing their own solar panels has helped boost the solar share of Pakistan's electricity from 1% to 28%.
articles.content:
Jewellery, glimmering silverware, sofas and an air-conditioning unit. Three months after his wedding, Faisal Shahzad's home in rural Punjab is bursting with gifts from his bride's family, as part of the dowry.

But the most prized possession is tucked under the bed: a 340W solar panel.

"In the summer we ran it from 08:00 in the morning until the evening," he says, adding they didn't need to use grid power at all during the day. "We ran our air cooler on it all day."

Pakistan has seen a boom in imported solar panels, which glisten from the rooftops of homes and hospitals; from farmers' fields to industrial complexes.

From 2018 to 2025, the share of electricity generated from solar energy in the country rose from 1% to 28%, according to Pakistan-based think tank Renewables First, with some seven million households now owning panels.

People used to gift motorbikes or other household items at weddings, Shahzad says. "Now they give a solar panel and an air cooler. It has almost become a must."

Alongside the solar panel he still uses the national grid to meet his energy needs, particularly as he lives in a house with his family and brothers' families, who often use multiple appliances simultaneously. But in a country where the average wage is just under 40,000 Pakistani rupees (£110; $145) per month, bills are becoming unaffordable, rising to 15,000-18,000 rupees.

This year, COP31 is pushing the world to move away from fossil-powered vehicles, boilers and other greenhouse gas-emitting equipment. And while Pakistan has become a poster child for solarisation, the national grid system is experiencing knock-on eﬀects.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant and inspiring increase in solar energy adoption in Pakistan, with solar power rising from 1% to 28% of the national electricity share due to widespread household solar panel installations. This shift has broad positive environmental impact by reducing reliance on fossil fuels and making energy more affordable and sustainable for millions, representing meaningful progress in renewable energy adoption with clear societal benefits.
articles.personality_title: Pakistan’s solar energy use jumps from 1% to 28%, changing homes and the grid
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Pakistan has traditionally relied on fossil fuels and the national power grid for electricity. Many homes faced high energy bills and unreliable power, especially in rural areas.

**What happened** – From 2018 to 2025, Pakistan saw a huge increase in solar panel installations by ordinary people. Now about seven million households have solar panels. This has raised the share of solar energy in the country’s electricity from just 1% to 28%. For example, Faisal Shahzad, a man in rural Punjab, uses a 340-watt solar panel to power his home’s air cooler all day without needing grid electricity.

**Impact** – This growth in solar power has helped people save money on electricity bills and rely less on fossil fuels. Solar panels have become popular gifts at weddings, showing how common and valuable they are. However, the rapid rise in solar use is causing challenges for Pakistan’s national power grid, which was not prepared for so many homes generating their own electricity.

**What’s next step** – Pakistan will need to improve and adapt its national grid to handle more solar power from homes. This may include better technology and policies to balance energy supply. The country’s experience also offers lessons for others looking to increase renewable energy use.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Pakistan’s widespread use of solar panels has quickly boosted clean energy while creating new challenges for the national power system.

articles.title: COP31: The push to protect warming oceans reaches the negotiating table
articles.summary: From identifying marine life with a cup of seawater to drawing on Indigenous knowledge to prevent wildfires, scientists and communities showcased both cutting-edge and time-tested ways to protect nature at COP31 on Tuesday. Yet turning innovation into action remains a challenge, with funding gaps persisting and ministers struggling to bridge divisions over fossil fuels and climate finance as negotiations enter their final days.
articles.content:
Today at COP31

Oceans: New research finds that more than 95 per cent of coastal and island nations include ocean measures in their climate plans.

New research finds that more than 95 per cent of coastal and island nations include ocean measures in their climate plans. Nature: Twenty-three countries endorse a wildfire prevention plan that draws on Indigenous knowledge and science.

Twenty-three countries endorse a wildfire prevention plan that draws on Indigenous knowledge and science. Climate impacts: Dominica, Myanmar and Honduras top a new ranking of countries hardest hit by extreme weather over 30 years.

Dominica, Myanmar and Honduras top a new ranking of countries hardest hit by extreme weather over 30 years. Negotiations: A draft text leaves ministers with major differences to resolve before Friday’s deadline. COP31 is set to close on 20 November.

Bob Marley’s Get Up, Stand Up greeted ministers arriving at COP31 in Antalya on Tuesday, as protesters urged them to fight for climate justice.

“Standing up” is the easy part. Reaching agreement is proving considerably harder.

The 18-page draft cover decision circulated on Monday remains a maze of competing proposals, while ministers take turns outlining national priorities in the plenary.

Away from the wrangling over text, the day’s spotlight fell on oceans and forests, nature’s great climate defenders, now facing mounting pressure from the very crisis they help contain.

Will the ocean make the final cut?

Despite their critical role in regulating the climate, oceans have often been overlooked in international climate negotiations. Now, they feature prominently in the first draft of a possible COP31 deal, reflecting efforts by co-hosts Australia and Türkiye to strengthen ocean-related climate action.

Whether those provisions survive the final round of negotiations, however, remains uncertain.

For Marine Lecerf, Head of International Policy at the Ocean and Climate Platform, the priority is not securing new commitments but delivering on existing ones.

“We’re not asking for a new mandate, we're asking for acceleration,” she told journalists on Tuesday.

A new analysis presented at COP31 underscores that challenge. More than 95 per cent of coastal and island nations now include ocean-related measures in their national climate plans, the study found. Yet around 60 per cent of those commitments depend on additional financing or technical support.

For Brianna Fruean, a Pacific youth climate envoy, that funding gap is already being felt by communities taking adaptation into their own hands.

In Fiji, for example, residents of Naidiri village have financed their own marine protected area, restoring coral reefs and fish stocks to safeguard the waters on which they depend.

“They shouldn't be taking money out of their own pockets to pay for these adaptation measures,” she said.

UN News/Laura Quiñones

What a cup of seawater can tell us

The ocean has been one of humanity's greatest allies against climate change, absorbing around 90 per cent of the excess heat generated by global warming. But that protection comes at a cost, as warming waters threaten coral reefs, fisheries and coastal communities.

Yet much of the ocean remains unexplored.

“Satellites cannot see beyond the surface of the ocean,” Joanna Post, Head of Ocean Observations at UNESCO’s Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission, told UN News.

“We’ve only mapped about 28 per cent of the seafloor. And there are species out there we haven't yet discovered.”

To close those knowledge gaps, UNESCO and its partners are turning to an unlikely source: a cup of seawater.

Using environmental DNA, or ‘eDNA’, scientists can identify species from the genetic traces they leave behind. UNESCO's eDNA Expeditions programme is using the technology at 25 marine sites worldwide, with local communities and schoolchildren helping collect samples every three months.

As warming waters drive species into new habitats, the findings could help governments identify which marine areas most need protection.

But far more data is needed. At COP31, Canada and the European Union sought additional support for the OceanEye International Alliance, a partnership with UNESCO aimed at strengthening global ocean monitoring.

“Ocean observations and data have quietly informed decision-making for a long time,” Post said. “They’re often unrecognized, but they’re powerful.”

She called for sustained investment in ocean monitoring rather than continued reliance on short-term research projects.

Türkiye also unveiled its Marine Litter Action Platform on Tuesday, connecting pollution-prevention initiatives with expertise and financing, including efforts to tackle abandoned fishing nets that entangle turtles, seabirds and other marine wildlife.

© UNESCO/Justin Gilligan

Nature’s oldest technology

Meanwhile, in Chad, Indigenous communities have long relied on the stars, clouds and movements of animals to anticipate rains, droughts and other environmental changes.

“They are our best school and our best technology,” Indigenous climate advocate Hindou Oumarou Ibrahim told UN News, describing knowledge passed down through generations.

That same wisdom is helping countries rethink how they prepare for increasingly destructive wildfires.

At COP31, 23 countries endorsed the Antalya Action Plan on Integrated Fire Management, backed by the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), shifting the focus from fighting fires to preventing them.

“Learning from Indigenous Peoples’ traditional practices and uses of fire can really help teach us how to live with good fire,” FAO forestry expert Amy Duchelle told UN News.

The approach includes carefully managed burning to maintain healthier landscapes, reduce fuel loads and lower the risk of devastating wildfires.
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories

articles.personality_title: COP31 highlights new ocean and wildfire protections backed by science and Indigenous knowledge
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – At COP31, a global climate summit held in Antalya, Turkey, countries and scientists gathered to discuss ways to protect the environment, focusing on oceans and forests, which help control the climate.

articles.personality_title_fr: COP31 met en avant la protection des océans et la prévention des incendies grâce à la science et aux savoirs autochtones
articles.personality_presentation_fr:

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Une nouvelle étude a montré que plus de 95 % des pays côtiers et insulaires ont intégré des mesures de protection des océans dans leurs plans climatiques. Des scientifiques ont présenté une méthode utilisant l’ADN environnemental (eDNA) dans un échantillon d’eau de mer pour identifier la vie marine et suivre les changements causés par le réchauffement des océans. Par ailleurs, 23 pays ont adopté un plan de prévention des incendies s’appuyant sur les connaissances autochtones pour gérer le feu de manière sûre et ainsi éviter des incendies destructeurs.

**Impact** – Ces efforts sont importants car les océans absorbent la majeure partie de la chaleur excédentaire due au réchauffement, mais restent vulnérables. L’utilisation de l’eDNA aide à identifier et protéger les espèces marines. Le plan de prévention des incendies change l’approche, passant de la lutte contre les feux à leur prévention, ce qui peut sauver forêts et communautés. Cependant, beaucoup de pays ont besoin de financements et d’aide technique pour mettre ces plans en œuvre.

**Prochaines étapes** – Les négociations à la COP31 se poursuivront jusqu’au 20 novembre pour finaliser les accords. Les pays et organisations travailleront à fournir les financements et soutiens nécessaires pour réaliser ces plans de protection des océans et de prévention des incendies. Le suivi des océans et l’utilisation des savoirs traditionnels devraient se développer.

**En une phrase** – À la COP31, les pays ont fait progresser la protection des océans et la prévention des incendies en combinant science et savoirs autochtones, mais la mise en œuvre demande encore plus de soutien et de financements.
articles.personality_title_es: COP31 destaca nuevas protecciones para océanos e incendios basadas en ciencia y saberes indígenas
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En la COP31, una cumbre mundial sobre el clima en Antalya, Turquía, países y científicos se reunieron para discutir cómo proteger el medio ambiente, enfocándose en los océanos y bosques, que ayudan a regular el clima.

**Qué pasó** – Una nueva investigación mostró que más del 95 % de los países costeros e insulares incluyen medidas para proteger los océanos en sus planes climáticos. Científicos presentaron un método que usa ADN ambiental (eDNA) de una muestra de agua de mar para identificar la vida marina y observar cambios causados por el calentamiento de los océanos. Al mismo tiempo, 23 países aprobaron un plan para prevenir incendios forestales usando el conocimiento indígena sobre el manejo seguro del fuego.

**Impacto** – Estos esfuerzos son importantes porque los océanos absorben la mayor parte del calor extra del calentamiento global, pero son vulnerables. Usar eDNA ayuda a identificar y proteger especies marinas importantes. El plan de incendios cambia el enfoque de combatir el fuego a prevenirlo, lo que puede salvar bosques y comunidades. Sin embargo, muchos países necesitan más dinero y ayuda técnica para aplicar estos planes.

**Qué sigue** – Las negociaciones en la COP31 continuarán hasta el 20 de noviembre para finalizar acuerdos. Países y organizaciones trabajarán para proporcionar fondos y apoyo para implementar los planes de protección oceánica y prevención de incendios. Se espera que el monitoreo oceánico y el uso de conocimientos tradicionales crezcan.

articles.title: Bizarre deep-sea fish with a see-through head captured in stunning 4K
articles.summary: Deep-sea researchers have captured stunning new footage of an extraordinarily rare fish with a transparent head and rotating eyes nearly 2,000 feet beneath the ocean's surface. Known as the barreleye fish, this bizarre creature uses its upward-pointing eyes to spot prey before rotating them forward to track its next meal, all while a transparent dome protects them.
articles.content:
A rare encounter nearly 2,000 feet beneath the ocean's surface gave scientists an extraordinary opportunity to film one of the deep sea's most unusual creatures. Researchers from the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute (MBARI) spotted a barreleye fish (Macropinna microstoma), a mysterious species known for its transparent head and remarkable eyes that can rotate to track prey.

The discovery occurred during an expedition aboard the research vessel David Packard. It marked only the eleventh time MBARI scientists have encountered this elusive fish during nearly four decades of ocean exploration.

Members of MBARI's Biodiversity and Biooptics Team were investigating marine life approximately 90 kilometers (55 miles) offshore when they spotted the fish about 600 meters (1,970 feet) below the surface. Using the remotely operated vehicle (ROV) Doc Ricketts, the researchers were filming and collecting deep-sea organisms when the unexpected visitor appeared.

"Seeing a barreleye fish is a rare treat. Crew from across the ship joined the science team in the control room, mesmerized by this remarkable animal. Deep-sea animals capture the imagination, creating wonder and awe that we hope will inspire stewardship of the largest living space on Earth," said Senior Scientist Steven Haddock.

[See video link after end of article.]

A Surprise Encounter Deep in the Pacific Ocean

The discovery was an unexpected highlight of the eight-day Diving Deep for Delicate Drifters expedition. Haddock and his colleagues had primarily been investigating gelatinous marine animals, including jellyfish, siphonophores, and ctenophores, also known as comb jellies. Their research seeks to understand how these delicate organisms have evolved to survive in the open ocean at great depths.

To investigate life throughout the water column, the team combined blue-water scuba dives near the surface with remotely operated vehicle surveys hundreds of meters below. These complementary approaches allowed researchers to observe and collect animals living in very different parts of the ocean.

The barreleye appeared just as the day's underwater operations were coming to an end. The ROV pilots were "flying" Doc Ricketts toward the surface for recovery when Research Specialist Shannon Johnson noticed the unusual fish and immediately asked them to stop.

Most of the scientists had already moved to the ship's wet lab, where they were preparing to catalog specimens collected during the dive. When word spread about the sighting, they hurried back to the control room, accompanied by crew members eager to see the extraordinary animal. The rare encounter provided an exciting conclusion to a busy and productive week of exploration.

How the Barreleye Fish Uses Its Transparent Head to Hunt

The barreleye's strange appearance is more than a biological curiosity. Its unusual anatomy helps it find food in the ocean's twilight zone, a dimly lit region where sunlight is faint and spotting prey can be difficult.

Earlier observations by MBARI Senior Scientist Bruce Robison and Research Specialist Kim Reisenbichler helped scientists understand how this remarkable fish hunts.

Rather than constantly swimming in search of food, Macropinna can remain nearly motionless in the water, supported by its large fins, which provide both stability and precise control over its movements. Its tubular eyes normally point upward, allowing it to watch for the faint silhouettes of animals passing overhead.

Once the fish detects something worth eating, its eyes can rotate within a transparent dome of tissue covering the top of its head. This unusual ability allows the barreleye to maintain visual contact with prey as it changes position to capture it.

The clear, gelatinous covering serves another important purpose. Barreleyes can feed on small crustaceans trapped among the stinging tentacles of deep-sea siphonophores, which are colonial animals related to jellyfish. The protective dome helps shield the fish's sensitive eyes while it retrieves its meal.

Rare 4K Footage Reveals Extraordinary Details

Scientists were able to spend approximately 20 minutes watching the barreleye during the encounter. Using the high-resolution 4K camera aboard Doc Ricketts, they recorded unusually detailed views of its anatomy and movements.

The team also adjusted the vehicle's lighting to make the fish's transparent head shield easier to observe. These changes helped reveal the unusual structures that make this species so distinctive.

ROV Pilot/Technician Cameron Law brought Doc Ricketts close enough to capture additional footage with the vehicle's virtual reality camera. The resulting 3D stereo imagery provides another perspective on the fish and could eventually be used in educational programs and public outreach.

"Macropinna reminds us of the surprising ways that animals have adapted to thrive in the ocean's midwater," said Haddock. "So many of them survive by looking for subtle optical cues, like a shadow passing overhead, and this sets off evolutionary competition, pitting bioluminescent camouflage against increasingly sophisticated visual capabilities."

An Extraordinary Sighting After Nearly 7,000 Deep-Sea Dives

The rarity of the encounter becomes even more striking when considering MBARI's extensive exploration history. Over nearly 40 years, the institute has conducted approximately 7,000 remotely operated vehicle dives and accumulated more than 41,000 hours of deep-sea video. Despite that enormous effort, researchers have recorded just 11 encounters with Macropinna microstoma.

MBARI's previous sighting of Macropinna occurred in 2021. The latest encounter represents two important firsts for the institute: its first 4K footage of this species and its first observation of the fish from the new flagship research vessel David Packard.

MBARI scientists have also encountered other members of the barreleye family during their ocean expeditions. This summer, researchers working with Schmidt Ocean Institute in the mid-Atlantic Ocean recorded another unusual deep-sea species, the binocular fish (Winteria telescopa).

Together, these encounters provide rare opportunities to observe the remarkable adaptations that allow animals to survive far beneath the ocean's surface, where light is scarce and much of the marine environment remains unexplored.

The Diving Deep for Delicate Drifters expedition was supported through the David and Lucile Packard Foundation's longstanding commitment to MBARI's scientific research.

articles.personality_title_fr: Un poisson barreleye à tête transparente filmé en 4K dans les profondeurs de l’océan
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques de l’Institut de Recherche de l’Aquarium de la Baie de Monterey (MBARI) étudient les créatures des grandes profondeurs pour comprendre comment elles survivent dans les zones sombres de l’océan. Ils utilisent des robots sous-marins appelés véhicules télécommandés (ROV) pour explorer près de 600 mètres sous la surface.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Lors d’une expédition de huit jours à bord du navire de recherche David Packard, les chercheurs de MBARI ont aperçu un poisson barreleye rare avec une tête transparente et des yeux rotatifs. C’était seulement la onzième fois en 40 ans que MBARI voyait ce poisson. Ils ont filmé en vidéo 4K détaillée ce poisson grâce au ROV Doc Ricketts, montrant comment il utilise sa tête claire pour protéger ses yeux pendant la chasse.

**Impact** – Les images montrent que le poisson barreleye peut regarder vers le haut pour repérer ses proies, puis tourner ses yeux vers l’avant pour les suivre. Sa tête transparente agit comme un bouclier, l’aidant à se nourrir près d’animaux ressemblant à des méduses urticantes. Cette découverte apporte des connaissances importantes sur les adaptations des animaux des grandes profondeurs où la lumière est très faible.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques utiliseront ces nouvelles vidéos 3D et 4K pour mieux comprendre le comportement du barreleye et partager ces découvertes avec le public via des programmes éducatifs. La poursuite de l’exploration des profondeurs pourrait révéler d’autres créatures rares et aider à protéger ces environnements océaniques fragiles.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Pour la première fois, des scientifiques ont filmé en haute définition un poisson barreleye rare à tête transparente, montrant sa façon unique de chasser dans les profondeurs.
articles.personality_title_es: Pez barreleye raro con cabeza transparente filmado en 4K en las profundidades del océano
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Científicos del Instituto de Investigación del Acuario de la Bahía de Monterey (MBARI) estudian criaturas de aguas profundas para entender cómo sobreviven en zonas oscuras del océano. Usan robots submarinos llamados vehículos operados a distancia (ROV) para explorar casi 600 metros bajo la superficie.

**Qué pasó** – Durante una expedición de ocho días en el barco de investigación David Packard, los investigadores de MBARI avistaron un raro pez barreleye con cabeza transparente y ojos que giran. Esta fue solo la undécima vez en 40 años que MBARI vio este pez. Grabaron video detallado en 4K usando el ROV Doc Ricketts, mostrando cómo usa su cabeza clara para proteger sus ojos mientras caza.

**Impacto** – El video revela que el pez puede mirar hacia arriba para detectar presas y luego girar sus ojos hacia adelante para seguirlas. Su cabeza transparente funciona como un escudo, ayudándolo a alimentarse cerca de animales parecidos a medusas con tentáculos urticantes. Este hallazgo aporta información importante sobre cómo los animales de aguas profundas se adaptan a la poca luz.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos usarán los nuevos videos en 3D y 4K para entender mejor el comportamiento del barreleye y compartir estos descubrimientos con el público a través de programas educativos. La exploración continua puede revelar más criaturas raras y ayudar a proteger estos frágiles ambientes marinos.

**Frase clave** – Por primera vez, científicos filmaron en alta definición un raro pez barreleye de cabeza transparente, mostrando su forma única de cazar en las profundidades.
